title: Differentiable Task Graph Learning: Procedural Activity Representation and Online Mistake Detection from Egocentric Videos
tldr: Make the task graph a differentiable parameter instead of a hand-built artifact, and the same graph that represents the procedure also flags mistakes online.

problem.task: Learn a partial ordering over key-steps from observed sequences, then use it to detect mistakes as they happen.

inputs.name: key-step sequence
inputs.chars: Observed so far; the causal setting means no future frames.

inputs.name: step embeddings
inputs.chars: Text or video features, in the feature-based variant.

outputs.name: task graph
outputs.chars: Edge weights are learned parameters — human-readable as a partial order.

outputs.name: mistake flag
outputs.chars: Current step violates the learned ordering.

training.supervision: Direct maximum-likelihood on edge weights from observed key-step sequences.
training.note: Because it is differentiable, the graph can be a layer inside a larger network rather than a preprocessing step.

method.intuition: A task graph is just a set of edge weights, so optimize them directly instead of hand-crafting an extraction procedure.
components: feature-based graph prediction from text or video embeddings

experiments.headline: +16.7% task graph accuracy over prior work on CaptainCook4D, and +19.8% / +7.5% mistake detection on Assembly101-O and EPIC-Tent-O.

why: The clearest demonstration that a symbolic procedure representation and a neural pipeline do not have to be separate systems.

title: Video-Mined Task Graphs for Keystep Recognition in Instructional Videos
tldr: Mine how people actually order steps across thousands of how-to videos, then use that distribution to regularize keystep recognition in a new video.

problem.task: Zero-shot keystep localization in an unseen instructional video.

inputs.name: video
inputs.chars: How-to video for a known task.

inputs.name: keystep list
inputs.chars: From a task vocabulary; the ordering is not given.

outputs.name: keystep assignment
outputs.chars: Per-segment, regularized by the mined graph.

training.supervision: The graph is mined from unlabeled how-to video corpora. Recognition itself stays zero-shot.
training.note: Probabilistic ordering, not a rigid script — that flexibility is the difference from earlier procedure-alignment work.

method.intuition: People do not follow recipes in a fixed order, so a script is the wrong prior and a distribution over orderings is the right one.
components: automatic task graph discovery from how-to video

experiments.headline: More reliable zero-shot keystep localization and better video representations than prior work across multiple instructional datasets.

why: Establishes the probabilistic-ordering view of procedure that the differentiable and online-mistake work later builds on.

title: Neural Task Graphs: Generalizing to Unseen Tasks from a Single Video Demonstration
tldr: Put a conjugate task graph between the demonstration and the policy, and one video is enough to do a task the model has never seen.

problem.task: One-shot visual imitation of a compositional task.

inputs.name: demo video
inputs.chars: A single demonstration of a task never seen in training.

outputs.name: conjugate task graph
outputs.chars: Nodes are actions, edges are states — the inverse of the usual convention.

training.supervision: Task-graph structure plus action supervision on seen tasks only.
training.note: Generalization is measured on task compositions absent from training, not on new instances of the same task.

method.intuition: A policy that maps a demonstration straight to actions has to relearn structure every time. Making the structure an explicit intermediate lets it be recombined.

experiments.headline: Inter-task generalization on two compositional benchmarks with better data efficiency, and task structure prediction that transfers to surgical video.

why: The historical root of the task-graph line, and a reminder that this idea started on the robot side.

title: HiERO: understanding the hierarchy of human behavior enhances reasoning on egocentric videos
tldr: Activity hierarchy falls out of unscripted video if you align clips to their narrations at several scales at once. Zero-shot then beats fully supervised procedure learning.

problem.task: Enrich video-segment features with hierarchical activity threads, for retrieval, grounding and procedure learning.

outputs.name: hierarchy-aware features
outputs.chars: Used with minimal extra training on downstream tasks.

training.supervision: Weak — alignment between video clips and their narrated descriptions.
training.note: No procedure labels at any point, which is why the zero-shot procedure-learning result is meaningful.

method.intuition: Human activity varies wildly on the surface but is generated by a hierarchy of related actions, and that hierarchy is recoverable from narration alignment alone.

experiments.headline: State of the art on all benchmarks, and +12.5% F1 on EgoProceL zero-shot over fully supervised methods.

why: Argues that procedure structure need not be annotated. It is already latent in how people narrate what they are doing.

title: P-JEPA: Procedural Video Representation Learning via Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture
tldr: Turning the stove on and off look identical. JEPA over a frame-aligned action space with pooled latent targets lets a 30-minute procedure fit in one model.

problem.task: Long-duration procedural video representation learning and temporal action segmentation.

inputs.name: long video features
inputs.chars: Videos over 30 minutes; features from V-JEPA 2, TSM or I3D — backbone-agnostic.

outputs.name: frame-aligned representation
outputs.chars: Probed by linear separability and streaming segmentation.

training.supervision: Self-supervised: predict pooled masked latent vectors in a dense frame-aligned action space.
training.note: The pooling is what dodges the quadratic attention cost that keeps other video models from seeing a whole procedure.

method.intuition: Procedural steps depend on context that arrived thirty minutes earlier, and a model that cannot hold that window cannot tell two visually identical actions apart.

experiments.headline: State of the art on Ego-Exo4D fine-grained action classification with an order of magnitude fewer parameters than LLM-based alternatives.

why: Carries the JEPA idea from generic video into procedure, where the long-range dependency is the whole problem.

title: ASHiTA: Automatic Scene-grounded Hierarchical Task Analysis
tldr: Decomposing a high-level instruction depends on the room you are standing in, so build the task hierarchy and the 3D scene graph together instead of in sequence.

problem.task: Turn an abstract instruction into grounded subtasks tied to specific objects in a specific 3D scene.

inputs.name: high-level task
inputs.chars: Abstract enough that it names nothing in the scene.

outputs.name: task hierarchy
outputs.chars: Subtasks, each attached to scene-graph nodes.

outputs.name: 3D scene graph
outputs.chars: Built task-driven, so it contains what the task needs.

training.note: The alternation matters: the graph decides what the decomposition can refer to, and the decomposition decides what the graph must contain.

method.intuition: Hierarchical task analysis is environment-dependent, so doing it before you have a scene representation gets you subtasks the robot cannot execute.
components: alternating task analysis and scene graph construction

experiments.headline: Substantially better than LLM baselines at environment-dependent decomposition, with grounding comparable to dedicated 3D grounding methods.

why: Shows procedure structure and scene structure are the same problem once you have to execute rather than describe.

title: Every Mistake Counts in Assembly
tldr: Build the constraint set from the mistakes you have already watched: spatial beliefs about how parts fit, temporal beliefs about what must come first, updated online.

problem.task: Identify ordering mistakes in an assembly sequence, online.

inputs.name: action sequence
inputs.chars: Observed so far, real-world and noisy.

outputs.name: ordering violation
outputs.chars: Checked against the current belief sets.

training.supervision: Beliefs are accumulated from observed mistakes rather than fit offline.
training.note: Episodic memory means the knowledge base grows during deployment — a rare instance of the adapt stage actually being implemented.

method.intuition: You cannot enumerate every wrong ordering in advance, but you can accumulate the constraints that the wrong ones violate.
method.backbone: belief-set knowledge base with episodic memory
components: new coarse part-position annotations for Assembly101

baselines: sequence models without an explicit knowledge base
experiments.headline: Inferred spatial and temporal beliefs identify incorrect orderings in real action sequences, outperforming the compared inference algorithms on Assembly101.

why: The clearest statement that a task assistant should keep learning its constraints while it watches, during deployment.

title: Action Genome: Actions as Composition of Spatio-temporal Scene Graphs
tldr: An action is a sequence of changing object relationships. Annotating those relationships gives few-shot recognition for free.

problem.task: Decompose actions into spatio-temporal scene graphs, and predict those graphs from video.

training.supervision: Dense object and relationship annotations on Charades video.
training.note: The relationship track is the reusable part. The action labels came with the source dataset.

method.intuition: Cognitive science says people encode events as part structures. The prototypical part is an action-object interaction, so annotate those.
method.backbone: scene-graph feature banks over an action recognition model

experiments.headline: 42.7% mAP few-shot action recognition with as few as 10 examples, by decomposing the temporal change in visual relationships.

why: The symbolic ancestor of object-centric procedural understanding, and still the cleanest argument for why decomposition helps.
